_comment: R&D decisions (ui-spec.md component 26, user's idea 2026-10-10). Ids are kept in saved state and turn reports: never rename or reuse one. Sizes are relative: RELIABILITY in seasons of the component's R&D gain, FUNDS and an option's cost as a share of a season's funding. Text fits both agencies; {name} and {second} are the people an option took. The first build has two or three per type; the pools grow after the play test (design.md 5).

decisions.headline: Pay for a static test firing?
decisions.text: The engine team wants to bolt the stage to the test stand and fire it, held down, before anything else is built around it. A clean run would settle a lot of arguments.

options.label: Pay for the full firing
options.shows: 70 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: The firing went clean
outcomes.text: The stage ran its full time without a flicker in the gauges. The engineers want to push it harder next time.

outcomes.headline: A rough run
outcomes.text: The engine shut down early on a sensor fault. The data is thin, but something was learned.

options.label: Fire it at half power
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: A careful half-power run
outcomes.text: Nothing dramatic, nothing broken, and a little more known about the engine.

outcomes.headline: No firing this time
outcomes.text: The stage goes back to the assembly hall untested.

decisions.recall: Last time the held-down firing went clean.
decisions.headline: Fire it at full thrust
decisions.text: Encouraged by the clean firing, the engine team wants to run the stage at full thrust for its whole burn time. If it holds, the design is proven; if it doesn't, the test stand may need rebuilding.

options.label: Run it at full thrust
options.shows: 60 % chance of about three seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Full thrust, full time
outcomes.text: The stage roared for its whole burn and shut down on command. The crew on the stand cheered.

outcomes.headline: A turbine let go
outcomes.text: A turbine blade failed at full speed and took the pump with it. The engineers will spend weeks on what is left.

outcomes.headline: Not yet
outcomes.text: The full-thrust run is put off.

decisions.recall: The full-thrust firing held all the way.
decisions.headline: One last endurance run
decisions.text: The engine has passed every firing so far. One long run, twice the burn time, would show where it wears out first.

options.label: Run it twice as long
options.shows: 50 % chance of about four seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season and a half's.

outcomes.headline: It just kept going
outcomes.text: The engine ran twice its burn time and came off the stand scorched but whole. The design is settled.

outcomes.headline: The chamber burned through
outcomes.text: Late in the run the chamber wall burned through. Now everyone knows where it wears out, and it cost an engine.

outcomes.headline: Enough testing
outcomes.text: The engine goes into production as it is.

decisions.headline: A week in the vacuum chamber?
decisions.text: The test lab has a free slot in its vacuum chamber. A week of airless cold and heat would show how the craft copes in space before it ever goes there.

options.label: Book the chamber
options.shows: 75 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: A week in space, on the ground
outcomes.text: Every system worked through the cold nights and hot days. The lab offers a longer run.

outcomes.headline: The chamber leaked
outcomes.text: A seal in the chamber failed on the second day and the test was stopped. Half a week of data is better than none.

options.label: Let another team have the slot

outcomes.headline: The slot goes elsewhere
outcomes.text: Another team takes the chamber.

decisions.recall: Last time the craft came through a week in the vacuum chamber.
decisions.headline: A month in the chamber
decisions.text: The lab can keep the craft in vacuum for a month: as long as a real mission. It would find the slow faults a week can't.

options.label: Keep it in for a month
options.shows: 65 % chance of about three seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: A month without a fault
outcomes.text: Thirty days of vacuum and the craft is still talking to the ground station.

outcomes.headline: A slow leak cooked the electronics
outcomes.text: In the third week a coolant leak ruined the electronics box. It will have to be rebuilt.

outcomes.headline: Enough of the chamber
outcomes.text: The craft goes back to the assembly room.

decisions.headline: Pay for a second round of inspections?
decisions.text: The quality office wants every weld and wire checked twice. It would slow nobody down, but the inspectors have to be paid.

options.label: Pay for the inspections
options.shows: Sure to give about a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: Faults found before they flew
outcomes.text: The inspectors find a cracked bracket and two loose connectors. Nobody likes being checked, but everyone is glad.

outcomes.headline: One round of checks
outcomes.text: The work goes on as it was.

decisions.headline: Balloon tanks on the pad
decisions.text: The night crew let the pressure drop in the rocket's thin-walled tanks while it stood empty on the pad. The chief engineer storms in and asks the room what would have happened.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: It would crumple under its own weight

outcomes.headline: Exactly right
outcomes.text: The tanks are held up by their own pressure, like a balloon. The chief engineer nods and puts a pressure alarm on every pad.

options.label: Nothing: the steel holds it up

outcomes.headline: Wrong, and costly
outcomes.text: The steel is thinner than paper in places. The engineers lose a week convincing the night crew to take the pressure seriously.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The tanks were empty. The real danger goes unaddressed, and a second scare follows the next week.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The chief engineer explains it and moves on.

decisions.headline: Three valves in a row
decisions.text: A design review stops at a part with three valves that all have to work, each tested at 95 % reliable. The reviewer asks how reliable the three are together.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The team signs off a part far weaker than it thinks. It shows up in testing a month later.

outcomes.headline: Right: the odds multiply
outcomes.text: Three parts that must all work are only as good as the product of their odds. The team redesigns it with two valves in parallel.

options.label: Over 99 %: three are safer than one

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: That's true of spares that back each other up, not of parts that must all work. The weak spot stays in the design.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The reviewer works it through on the blackboard.

decisions.headline: Why so blunt?
decisions.text: A visiting official asks why the craft's heat shield is round and blunt instead of pointed like a bullet. The engineers look to you for the answer.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Pointed would cut through the air and heat up less

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: A pointed shape keeps the hot shock wave right against the skin. The official leaves with the wrong idea and asks for a redesign study.

options.label: The blunt shape pushes a shock wave out ahead and keeps the heat off

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: Most of the heat stays in the air the shock wave pushes aside. The official is impressed, and so are the engineers.

outcomes.headline: Not the reason
outcomes.text: Room is a side effect. The engineers spend an afternoon setting the record straight.

outcomes.headline: The engineers explain
outcomes.text: The chief designer gives the official a short talk on shock waves.

decisions.headline: The night shift wants a say
decisions.text: The technicians on the night shift say nobody asks them anything, though they build most of the hardware. They want a meeting with the design team. The foreman says they should mind their benches.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: They had good ideas
outcomes.text: The technicians bring a list of small fixes that make the hardware easier to build right. The design team takes most of them.

outcomes.headline: A night of grievances
outcomes.text: The meeting turns into a list of complaints about pay and canteen food. Nothing useful comes of it, and the foreman feels undermined.

outcomes.headline: Order kept
outcomes.text: The night shift goes back to work. It's quieter than before.

outcomes.headline: A sullen night shift
outcomes.text: The technicians do exactly what they are told and nothing more. Small mistakes creep in.

outcomes.headline: A bonus goes a long way
outcomes.text: The night shift takes the money and the hint. The hardware coming off the benches is tidier.

outcomes.headline: They wanted to be heard, not paid
outcomes.text: The technicians feel bought off. The design team hears about it for weeks.

decisions.headline: Who gets the credit?
decisions.text: A fix that solved a stubborn problem came out of a late-night argument between two engineers. The agency magazine wants a name for its cover story.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: The whole team on the cover
outcomes.text: The photo of the team hangs in every office. People talk about the next fix already.

outcomes.headline: Credit spread thin
outcomes.text: The one who really cracked it feels passed over. The mood on the team sours.

options.label: Keep it out of the magazine

outcomes.headline: No story
outcomes.text: The fix goes into the drawings and nobody's name goes into print.

outcomes.headline: A star is made
outcomes.text: The lead engineer is fired up by the attention and drives the team hard.

outcomes.headline: Resentment
outcomes.text: The others know who really did it. The team stops talking at lunch.

decisions.headline: Who will oversee the test firing?
decisions.text: The test stand is booked for a firing of the stage, but its usual test conductor is ill. Somebody has to run the countdown, read the gauges and call the abort if it comes to that.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance of a clean run.

outcomes.headline: {name} ran a clean test
outcomes.text: {name} called every step on time and caught a sticking valve before ignition. The firing told the team what it needed.

outcomes.headline: {name} aborted too late
outcomes.text: {name} hesitated over a warning light, and the engine ran rough for two seconds too long. Parts of the stand need replacing.

options.label: Nobody, the test is put off

outcomes.headline: The firing is put off
outcomes.text: The stand stays booked for later.

decisions.headline: Who signs off the vibration test?
decisions.text: The shake table is ready to rattle the hardware the way a launch would. Somebody experienced has to decide how hard to shake it and what counts as a pass.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance the test finds the weak spots.

outcomes.headline: {name} found the weak spot
outcomes.text: {name} ran the table hard enough to shake a bracket loose on the ground instead of in flight.

outcomes.headline: {name} shook it to pieces
outcomes.text: {name} set the table too hard and broke a test unit that was fine.

options.label: Run the standard test
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: A standard shake
outcomes.text: The book test passes without surprises.

decisions.headline: Freeze the design?
decisions.text: The chief designer wants to stop changing the drawings and build what's there. The engineers say the open issues will cost something now, but the work would go faster after.

options.label: Freeze the design
options.shows: About a season's gain lost now, then R&D 30 % faster for four seasons.

outcomes.headline: The design is frozen
outcomes.text: The open issues are written up and set aside. The workshops start building to one set of drawings.

options.label: Start a redesign
options.shows: About a season and a half's gain lost now, then R&D 40 % faster for six seasons.

outcomes.headline: Back to the drawing board
outcomes.text: The team throws out the weak parts of the design and starts them again, properly.

outcomes.headline: Refining as before
outcomes.text: The drawings keep changing week by week.

decisions.headline: A sprint on overtime?
decisions.text: The team could work evenings and weekends for a while. The hardware would move faster; the people would get tired.

options.label: Go on overtime
options.shows: R&D 50 % faster for two seasons; the team's morale drops.

outcomes.headline: Lights on all night
outcomes.text: The workshop never closes. The work races ahead, and the coffee runs out by Thursday.

outcomes.headline: Normal hours
outcomes.text: The team goes home on time.

decisions.headline: Shutdown at second 41
decisions.text: On the last test firing the engine shut itself down 41 seconds into a 60-second run. The engineers have three clues and three suspects.

clues.text: Chamber pressure fell steadily for two seconds before the shutdown.
Turbopump vibration stayed normal the whole run.
The igniter fired twice at the start before the engine lit.

decisions.stakes: The right cause is worth about two seasons' gain; chasing the wrong one costs a season's.

outcomes.headline: Not the bearing
outcomes.text: The pump comes apart in perfect shape. The vibration data said so all along.

outcomes.headline: The valve it was
outcomes.text: A spring in the fuel valve was too weak and let it drift shut. Falling pressure, then shutdown: it fits. A stiffer spring fixes it.

outcomes.headline: A red herring
outcomes.text: The double ignition was harmless; the engine lit fine. The team loses a season rebuilding an igniter that worked.

outcomes.headline: More data first
outcomes.text: The fault stays open until the next firing.

decisions.headline: The battery dies in the chamber
decisions.text: In the vacuum chamber the craft's power fails after a few hours. On the bench it runs for days. The engineers have four clues.

clues.text: The battery holds its voltage for days at room temperature.
In the chamber the voltage sags after the third hour, as the craft cools.
The heater's thermostat is mounted right beside the warm transmitter.
The transmitter draws its normal current throughout.

decisions.stakes: The right cause is worth about two seasons' gain; chasing the wrong one costs a season's.

outcomes.headline: The cells were fine
outcomes.text: New cells fail the same way. The bench test had already cleared them.

outcomes.headline: It was freezing
outcomes.text: The thermostat sat by the warm transmitter, so it never switched the heater on, and the cold battery gave out. Moving it fixes the craft.

outcomes.headline: Not the radio
outcomes.text: The radio's current was normal all along. A redesigned transmitter changes nothing.

outcomes.headline: More data first
outcomes.text: The fault stays open until the next chamber run.

decisions.headline: The air force lends its altitude chamber
decisions.text: The air force offers its high-altitude test chamber for a month. The catch: it wants one of the team's engineers on loan for two seasons in return.

options.label: Accept, and send an engineer
options.shows: About three seasons' gain at once; the engineer is away for two seasons.

outcomes.headline: A month at altitude
outcomes.text: The chamber shows what a month of tests at home never could. {name} packs a bag for the air base.

outcomes.headline: Thanks, but no
outcomes.text: The chamber goes to someone else.

decisions.headline: A cheaper part, untested
decisions.text: A new supplier offers a part at a third of the usual price, available now. Nobody has flown it yet.

options.label: Take the cheaper part
options.shows: Saves money; 60 % chance it works out, else about a season and a half's gain lost.

outcomes.headline: It works as well as the old one
outcomes.text: The new part passes every test, and the savings go back into the budget.

outcomes.headline: You get what you pay for
outcomes.text: The part fails its third test. The old supplier has to be called back, at the old price and with a delay.

outcomes.headline: The usual supplier
outcomes.text: The usual parts arrive at the usual price.

decisions.headline: Who works with whom?
decisions.text: A tricky interface between two subsystems needs two engineers who will talk to each other. Pick a pair; how well they get on decides how it goes.
decisions.stakes: A good pair is worth about two seasons' gain and grows closer; a bad one clashes.

outcomes.headline: {name} and {second} cracked it
outcomes.text: {name} and {second} worked it out over two long evenings and came out friends.

outcomes.headline: {name} and {second} clashed
outcomes.text: {name} and {second} argued over every drawing. The interface is still a mess, and so is their working relationship.

options.label: Leave the team as it is

outcomes.headline: As it was
outcomes.text: The interface is worked on in the usual way.

decisions.headline: An old hand and a new one
decisions.text: The training office suggests pairing two engineers for a season so one can learn from the other. It only works if they get along.
decisions.stakes: A good pair is worth about a season's gain and grows closer; a bad one clashes.

outcomes.headline: {second} learned a lot from {name}
outcomes.text: The two spend the season side by side, and the questions get better every week.

outcomes.headline: {name} and {second} didn't get on
outcomes.text: One lectured, the other stopped listening. They ask to be split up.

outcomes.headline: No pairing
outcomes.text: Everyone works as before.

decisions.headline: The rival's engine runs cooler
decisions.text: The Intelligence Office reports that the rival agency cools its engine by running fuel through the chamber walls before burning it. Our engineers could try the same.
decisions.stakes: If the tip is right, about three seasons' gain; if it's wrong, about a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: The tip was good
outcomes.text: Fuel through the walls keeps the chamber cool enough to run longer and harder. The engineers wonder why they didn't think of it.

outcomes.headline: The tip was garbled
outcomes.text: The report mixed up two different engines. The team loses a season on a design that was never going to work.

outcomes.headline: Our own way
outcomes.text: The report goes in a drawer.

decisions.headline: The rival's craft stays warm
decisions.text: The Intelligence Office says the rival wraps its craft in layers of thin metallised film to keep its warmth in. Our engineers could copy it.
decisions.stakes: If the tip is right, about three seasons' gain; if it's wrong, about a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: Wrapped up warm
outcomes.text: Layers of film keep the craft's temperature steady through the night side. The tip was right.

outcomes.headline: Wrong film, wrong place
outcomes.text: The film the report described traps heat where it shouldn't. The electronics overheat in testing.

outcomes.headline: Our own way
outcomes.text: The report goes in a drawer.

decisions.headline: A week on the big test stand
decisions.text: The engine test centre has its largest stand free for a week. The engineers want a short campaign on the engines: firings, then the measurements that make sense of them, planned shift by shift. You can plan it yourself, or let the team run it their way.

options.label: Run it yourself
options.shows: Opens the campaign. The objective is worth about a season and a half of R&D, the bonus about three; falling short costs nothing but the chance.

outcomes.headline: A week to remember on the big stand
outcomes.text: Six firings and the measurements to match. The engines' start-up is better understood than it has ever been.

outcomes.headline: A good week on the big stand
outcomes.text: Enough firings and enough data to settle the questions the engineers came with.

outcomes.headline: Not enough on the big stand
outcomes.text: Too few firings to tell the engineers what they wanted to know. The week was not wasted, but it changed nothing.

outcomes.headline: The team's own way
outcomes.text: The team ran a quiet week of routine firings. Nothing new came of it.

decisions.headline: A week in the vacuum chamber
decisions.text: The big vacuum chamber is free for a week. The engineers want to run the craft through it as it will fly: runs in the cold and the vacuum, then the measurements that make sense of them, planned shift by shift. You can plan it yourself, or let the team run it their way.

options.label: Run it yourself
options.shows: Opens the campaign. The objective is worth about a season and a half of R&D, the bonus about three; falling short costs nothing but the chance.

outcomes.headline: A week to remember in the chamber
outcomes.text: Six runs and the measurements to match. The craft's systems are better understood than they have ever been.

outcomes.headline: A good week in the chamber
outcomes.text: Enough runs and enough data to settle the questions the engineers came with.

outcomes.headline: Not enough in the chamber
outcomes.text: Too few runs to tell the engineers what they wanted to know. The week was not wasted, but it changed nothing.

outcomes.headline: The team's own way
outcomes.text: The team ran a quiet week of routine checks in the chamber. Nothing new came of it.
